**Case Vignette: "Elena"**

Elena is a 27-year-old Latin American woman who works as a freelance animator from her small apartment in a mid-sized city. She came to therapy at the urging of a close friend, who noticed she had stopped leaving her home except for grocery deliveries and had lost nearly ten pounds over three months. Elena sits in the session with her knees drawn up to her chest, even on the warmest days, and she keeps a clear line of sight to the door.

The trauma began eighteen months ago, when she was living with Marcos, a man she had dated for two years. He was charming at first—a graphic designer who admired her work and seemed to understand the creative life. The first incident happened after a gallery opening. Elena had spent the evening talking to an old classmate, and when they got home, Marcos accused her of flirting. She laughed it off, but he grabbed her wrist so hard it left a bruise. The next morning, he brought her coffee and cried, apologizing, telling her he was just so afraid of losing her. She believed him.

Over the next year, the pattern became a cycle she could predict but not escape. A minor disagreement—a dish left in the sink, a text she didn’t answer quickly enough—would escalate into a slammed door, a thrown object, a shove against the wall. Elena learned to read the temperature of his silences, to keep her voice low and her body small. She stopped calling her mother as often, stopped going to the studio where she used to work with other animators. She told herself she could manage it, that his love was real, that she just needed to be better.

The final night, he struck her across the face with an open hand, then with a closed fist. She remembers the sound of her own head hitting the tile floor of their bathroom. She remembers looking up at the ceiling fan spinning, thinking, *I will die here if I stay.* She left that night with only her laptop, her phone, and a small bag of clothes. She never went back.

Now, Elena lives alone. She works on animation projects for a children’s educational series, but she finds herself unable to draw faces—especially male faces. She sketches the same background scenes over and over: empty rooms, closed doors, windows with no view. Her deadlines are slipping, and her producer has sent two concerned emails. She cannot bring herself to reply. She feels a constant, low-grade static in her body, like her nerves are live wires. She startles at the sound of a motorcycle backfiring, at a knock on her neighbor’s door, at the vibration of her own phone.

She has not dated anyone since she left. She deleted all her social media accounts because she could not stop checking to see if Marcos had posted about her, or worse, if he had found a new girlfriend. She dreams of the bathroom floor, of the ceiling fan, of his hands. She wakes up with her own hands clenched into fists, her jaw aching from grinding her teeth.

The most difficult part, she tells me, is the shame. She cannot understand why she stayed. She is an intelligent woman—she creates entire worlds from nothing, frame by frame—yet she could not see the prison she was building for herself. She feels watched even when she is alone, and she has started sleeping with the lights on, a baseball bat beside her bed.

She has not spoken to her mother about what happened. Her mother would say she told her so. Elena cannot bear that. So she sits in my office, wrapped in a hoodie, her eyes fixed on the floor, and she tells me about the man who loved her and hurt her, and how she is still learning to believe that both things can be true.
